newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Further S.African rand strength seen limited.
newsitem.headline: Further S.African rand strength seen limited.

text.p: The South African rand appeared to be no longer significantly undervalued and further upside potential was limited, U.S. investment bank Salomon Brothers says in a research note.

The rand firmed to its strongest level in a month on Thursday when it touched a 4.39 bid against the dollar in the wake of what analysts have described as an investor friendly budget unveiled by Finance Minister Trevor Manuel on Wednesday.
In early Friday afternoon trade it was quoted at around the 4.4150 level.
Commenting on the budget, Salomon Brothers said that while the budget news appeared to be positive for the currency, further upside potential remained limited.
"At current levels, the rand appears no longer significantly undervalued, and the current account remains in deficit," it said.
Reserve Bank figures show South Africa recorded an unadjusted current account deficit of 50 million rand in the fourth quarter of 1996, compared with a 2.96 billion rand deficit in the third quarter.

Salomon Brothers said the Reserve Bank was concerned about any further erosion to South Africa's competitiveness following a nine percent real effective appreciation in the rand since the beinning of the year.
"At the same time, the Reserve Bank probably would counter further appreciation, in order to boost its reserves and reduce its forward losses."
However, the mixture of a restrictive budget and announcements on the further relaxation in exchange controls should continue to provide a favourable background for rand-denominated bonds.
"Thus, yields will reverse the recent backup, especially as consumer inflation probably will start to fall from May onwards."
Consumer inflation rose 9.4 percent year-on-year in January and is expected to peak at around 10 percent in the months ahead.
In the medium-term, slowing inflation, improving external balances and government's drive to curb public spending growth should allow a decline in ten-year yields to about 13.5 percent.

"At the same time, such developments should encourage the Reserve Bank to reduce official rates by 200 basis points before year-end, provided growth in money and credit resumes its deceleration," it said.
Some local economists have predicted that Bank rate, currently at 17 percent, could fall by as many as three percentage points this year, although most expect a two percentage point cut by year-end.
